items.title: Mapping University Students Risk of Dependence on Generative Artificial Intelligence Using K-Means Clustering
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has changed how university students approach academic tasks. Although these tools can support learning and improve efficiency, frequent reliance on them raises concerns about students' ability to study and solve problems independently. This study aims to identify patterns of GenAI use among university students and explore potential indicators of dependence through K-Means clustering. An exploratory quantitative approach was adopted, using questionnaire responses collected through 15 items measured on a five-point Likert scale. Of the 106 responses received, 104 met the inclusion criteria and were retained for analysis. The data underwent screening, numerical encoding, and reverse scoring before being grouped using the K-Means algorithm. The appropriate number of clusters was selected by comparing Silhouette Scores across solutions containing two to seven clusters. The analysis identified three student groups, with a Silhouette Score of 0.2443. The first group comprised 30 students (28.85%) who showed relatively higher GenAI use and stronger indications of behavioral dependence. The second group included 11 students (10.58%) who reported lower GenAI use but demonstrated limitations in academic independence and understanding. The remaining 63 students (60.58%) formed a group characterized by moderate GenAI use. These findings suggest that frequency of use alone does not adequately reflect the risk of dependence. However, the relatively low Silhouette Score indicates limited separation between groups, meaning that the resulting profiles should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive.

items.title: Mental Workload: Physiological Assessment and Validation Using Visual Stimuli
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper provides a notion for the use of electroencephalography (EEG) in the field of cognitive science. In particular, we investigated the brain activity of operators while spotting the differences in similar‐looking pictures at three levels of difficulty. As many practical loads are fundamentally intrinsic, the task was designed to specifically induce intrinsic workload (the productive load as per Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)). The experiment used the task: Spot the Difference to create a workload scenario comprising three difficulty levels: spotting five differences, three more differences, and two more differences (along with retaining the previous differences from working memory). The task was designed intrinsically as the operators are generally occupied with tasks involving working memory and requiring attention towards the varying number of resources. By utilising the brain signatures a mental workload model was developed employing a Support Vector Machine (SVM) as the classifier. The workload levels were classified within an accuracy range of 84% to 98% ( p < 0.05). Moreover, using subjective ratings about the workload on NASA's Task Load Index (NASA‐TLX) rating scale, workload scores were obtained for validation corresponding to the difficulty levels. Finally, a correlation study showed the association of different EEG features with the workload score within a correlation coefficient range of 0.306 to 0.748 ( p < 0.05 2‐tailed). The reported results can also provide new insights into the cognitive workload assessment of the operators at various phases of task loads. Findings of this type may lead to the industrial and professional measurement and improvement of cognitive aptitude soon.

items.title: Monad, Memory and Mind of Stars, Planets, and Biospheres
items.abstract: Contemporary discussion of mind usually takes the animal nervous system as its default bearer and thereby leaves unexamined how mind stands to scale. The two common responses — deflationary refusal of all mental predicates above the organism, and their inflationary projection across the cosmos — share a premise this article rejects: that mind is a single quantity, present or absent, greater or less. Within Informational Monism the article separates two independent axes and a third consideration that neither axis captures. Depth of hosting is the scale, dissipative throughput and fixity of the structure in the rendered bulk by which a boundary operator (the Holographic Monad) is held. Articulation is the rank, from passive record through maintained form, memory and experience to counterfactual sovereignty, to which that structure retains, uses and refines its history. The archetype of the host’s physical avatar fixes the order of the Monad at formation and is not altered by later development. Four terms are kept distinct: Monad (boundary operator), Soul (register at the Code Circuit), Consciousness (interface magnitude in the bulk), and Mind (structural competence measured by rank). On these axes stars, planets and biospheres separate cleanly and in opposite orders. A star is deepest and least articulated; a biosphere is shallower and the first to reach genuine memory and refined constraint; a human being is shallowest in depth and highest in articulation. The same framework yields a bridge to artificial intelligence that does not pass through the question of consciousness: a system may be highly articulated and almost without depth, or the reverse. Hosting is conditional on the maintenance of form against turnover, which excludes panpsychism by criterion rather than by disclaimer. The article is a hypothesis in natural philosophy. Its empirical ladder and comparisons stand if the postulates concerning Soul and Consciousness are set aside. Mind is not one quantity. Depth of hosting and articulation of rank are independent axes; archetype fixes Monadic order at formation. Four terms kept distinct: Monad (boundary operator), Soul (Code-Circuit register), Consciousness (bulk interface magnitude), Mind (structural competence by rank). Opposite orderings: stars are deepest and least articulated; humans are shallowest and most articulated; biospheres cross into memory first. Anti-panpsychism by criterion: only structures that maintain form against turnover (rank R2+) host; passive aggregates do not. Bridge to AI without the consciousness question: high articulation can coexist with near-zero intrinsic depth, and the reverse — placing geological, biospheric and artificial systems in one formal class. Keywords: Monad; hosting; depth and articulation; rank of mind; stars; planets; biosphere; memory; Soul; Consciousness; Threshold of Correspondence; artificial intelligence; philosophy of nature

items.title: NVIDIA Stock Price Forecasting in 2025 Using a Time-Series Based LSTM Model
items.abstract: Advances in computing technology, artificial intelligence, and graphics accelerators have driven significant growth in the value of NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) shares over the past decade. The high volatility and non-linear patterns in NVDA's stock price require the use of forecasting methods that can capture long-term dependencies in time-series data. This study proposes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to predict NVDA's stock price using historical daily data up to 2025. The training process was carried out using a two-layer LSTM architecture, Adam optimizers, and a 60-day time window. The evaluation results show that the model is capable of achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 4%, which indicates a high level of accuracy in predicting price movement patterns. Visualization of the prediction results confirms that the model successfully follows actual trends consistently, with relatively small deviations at extreme fluctuation points. Additionally, the model was used to project NVDA stock prices ten steps ahead, showing that price movement trends remain consistent with historical patterns. These findings contribute methodologically to studies on high-risk stock forecasting through deep learning approaches and provide a basis for data-driven decision-making in the modern financial sector.

items.title: Occupational health and safety performance in the geomatics profession: the role of digital ergonomics, safety culture and international benchmarking
items.abstract: This study investigates occupational health and safety (OHS) among geomatics professionals who alternate between terrain-based fieldwork and office-based digital tasks. A cross-sectional survey of 99 professionals in Uşak, Türkiye, was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, multiple linear regression and strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis. Slips and falls were reported by 28.1% of respondents, 37.5% considered protective equipment inadequate and 69% experienced musculoskeletal or visual discomfort during computer-based work. Although 81.3% had received OHS training, regular inspections covered only 53.1% of workplaces. Statistical analyses showed that training, equipment adequacy, ergonomic conditions, digital reporting and governance practices jointly shape OHS preparedness and perceived productivity. International benchmarking also indicated gaps in inspection coverage, equipment adequacy and digital integration. The findings demonstrate the dual physical and digital safety challenges of geomatics work and support stronger inspections, improved ergonomics, technology-oriented training, inclusive practices and sector-specific risk management for emerging geospatial technologies.

items.title: On the ROAD™ to Transparent AI Disclosure in Research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities continue to advance, and researchers increasingly use AI to help them reach their research goals. As a result, disclosing AI use has become essential. Yet researchers face a dilemma about whether to disclose how they used AI. Disclosure may reduce others' trust in their findings, while hiding AI use risks later discovery and damage to their reputation. I argue that researchers should disclose, and that effective disclosure begins with keeping a thorough record of their AI use, which I call an AI research footprint. I then introduce the ROAD™ framework (Request, Output, Assess, Decide), which helps researchers report what they asked AI to do, what it produced, how they assessed the output, and what they decided.

items.title: Oncogenic mutations in non-small cell lung cancer: from molecular mechanisms to clinical practice
items.abstract: Targeted therapy has revolutionized the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients harboring oncogenic alterations, and next-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) significantly increase blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, leading to improved disease control and survival benefits. However, several issues remain to be addressed, including the selection of more appropriate and individualized agents, the emergence of TKI resistance, and the challenging management of central nervous system (CNS) progression. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the efficacy and safety of TKIs and targeted specific antibodies in advanced or metastatic patients with common or rare mutations, providing guidance in selecting the optimal agent. We further explore the mechanisms underlying drug resistance and regimens aimed at overcoming resistance. In nonmetastatic resectable or unresectable NSCLC, we discuss the therapeutic potential of targeted agents and current issues requiring further research. In addition, we distinguish current and potential therapeutic strategies for patients with baseline brain metastasis (BM) and those without baseline BM who subsequently develop brain progression, leading to more effective and personalized treatment. Finally, we provide perspectives on challenges and future directions in the identification and treatment of oncogenic alterations, particularly in the context of co-mutations and the heterogeneous nature of metastases, and emphasize the clinical importance of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted genetic testing and biomarker development.

items.title: One Anti-ST2 Biologic, Three Gateways: What an Alarmin-Targeted Monoclonal Antibody Candidate's Regulatory Path Reveals About Parallel Health Canada, FDA, and EMA Clinical Trial Authorization
items.abstract: Anti-ST2 monoclonal antibodies neutralize the interleukin-33 receptor, blocking a key upstream alarmin signalling pathway implicated in airway inflammation, and represent a biologic class under continued investigation for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation reduction, an area with limited targeted biologic options relative to severe asthma. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of an anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. As a large-molecule biologic governed by ICH S6(R1) principles rather than the small-molecule nonclinical framework, this candidate illustrates how species-relevant pharmacology and immunogenicity considerations carry through the administrative layer of all three regions even though the core harmonized scientific content, Modules 2 through 5 of the Common Technical Document and their EU IMPD equivalent, remains substantially shared. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a respiratory biologic program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing monoclonal antibody candidates in chronic respiratory disease.Keywords: anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; ICH S6(R1); regulatory artificial intelligence

This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1/2 clinical trial of an ATR kinase inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using a biomarker-selected advanced solid tumour population as the illustrative scenario. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case across all three regions while the biomarker selection strategy itself, the companion diagnostic or laboratory-developed test used to identify eligible patients, introduces specific administrative and scientific considerations in each region's review. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a biomarker-driven oncology program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing DNA damage response-targeted oncology candidates across Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: ATR kinase inhibitor; DNA damage response; biomarker-selected oncology trial; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; regulatory artificial intelligence

items.title: One Bispecific Antibody-Drug Conjugate, Three Gateways: What a Dual-Target Oncology Candidate's Regulatory Path Reveals About Parallel Health Canada, FDA, and EMA Clinical Trial Authorization
items.abstract: Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) that simultaneously engage two distinct cell-surface receptors and deliver a cytotoxic payload represent one of the more structurally complex biologic modalities currently advancing through oncology development, combining the target-engagement logic of bispecific antibody engineering with the potency and bystander-effect considerations of conventional ADC payload chemistry. This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1b combination trial of a bispecific ADC candidate in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case for a complex biologic across all three regions, while each jurisdiction's administrative layer, Module 1 in Canada and the United States, Part II of the EU's Clinical Trials Information System filing, imposes region-specific requirements that a sponsor developing a combination-therapy oncology program cannot simply duplicate from one region to the next. The article addresses the particular operational challenges this modality and combination-trial design create, the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of complex, multi-document regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing bispecific ADC programs across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: bispecific antibody-drug conjugate; oncology combination therapy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; CTIS; regulatory artificial intelligence

items.abstract: Cardiac myosin inhibitors are a recently established mechanistic class that reduces excess cardiac contractility in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) by allosterically and reversibly modulating myosin motor activity, with the first agent in this class having received FDA approval in late 2025. This article uses a hypothetical new multicentre Phase 2 clinical trial of a follow-on cardiac myosin inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company unrelated to the approved product's marketing authorization holder, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. Because an approved product already exists in this class, the comparison pays particular attention to how each region's reviewers are expected to treat the established drug-drug interaction and echocardiographic monitoring precedent from that approved product's development when evaluating a new candidate acting through the same mechanism. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to developing a follow-on candidate in a class with an approved precedent, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing cardiac myosin inhibitor candidates across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: cardiac myosin inhibitor; obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; echocardiographic monitoring; regulatory artificial intelligence

items.abstract: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors are a class of oral small-molecule agents under continued clinical development for hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia, acting by inhibiting the transfer of cholesteryl esters from high-density lipoprotein to lower-density lipoprotein particles. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of a CETP inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. All three jurisdictions rely on the harmonized Common Technical Document (CTD) structure, under which Modules 2 through 5, covering quality, nonclinical, and clinical evidence, are substantially portable across regions, while Module 1 and its regional equivalents remain jurisdiction-specific. The article presents each region's legal framework, review timeline, and administrative content, develops a three-way comparison table, and then turns to the practical challenges a sponsor managing this triad of filings actually faces and the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are being used, and can responsibly be used, in regulatory document preparation, administration, and quality control across all three jurisdictions. The analysis closes with concrete recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing parallel CETP inhibitor trials, and more generally for any oral small-molecule cardiometabolic candidate filed simultaneously in Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: CETP inhibitor; dyslipidemia; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; Common Technical Document; regulatory artificial intelligence

items.title: Optical neural computing: from fourier optics to integrated photonic artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence have accelerated interest in optical computing as a high-speed and energy-efficient alternative to conventional electronic hardware. Fourier optical computing provides an important foundation for this field because operations including convolution, correlation, spectral transformation, and certain classes of linear transformation can be implemented through diffraction, interference, and Fourier-domain processing. This review traces the development of optical neural computing from classical 4-f processors and free-space diffractive systems to programmable optical neural networks, integrated photonic accelerators, reservoir-computing platforms, and field-programmable photonic architectures. The underlying physical principles, computational mechanisms, and hardware implementations are systematically examined, with particular attention to reconfigurable photonics, metasurfaces, diffractive deep learning, photonic integrated circuits, and hybrid optical–electronic systems. Emerging applications in computational imaging, autonomous sensing, edge intelligence, high-speed communications, and quantum-enabled information processing are critically discussed alongside challenges related to scalability, programmability, nonlinear computation, training, and system integration. By positioning Fourier optics as a foundational branch within the broader landscape of optical neural computing, this review highlights the convergence of free-space, integrated, programmable, and hybrid photonic technologies toward next-generation artificial-intelligence hardware.

items.title: Optimization of Deep Learning Approach Using Chaotic Algorithm for Hepatitis Detection
items.abstract: Hepatitis still remains one of the major health issues in the world and is responsible for a significant amount of morbidity and mortality due to diseases related to the liver. Traditional approaches for hepatitis detection are costly, laboratorial, time-consuming, and error-prone. While AI and DL have enhanced medical diagnosis significantly, current models are prone to problems such as overfitting, long convergence period, and lack of generalization, which are primarily associated with inefficiency of hyperparameter optimization. In this research, the authors propose the use of optimized deep learning model based on Chaotic Optimization Algorithm (COA) for hepatitis detection. This approach combines Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Deep Neural Network (DNN) models with the application of COA, which allows optimizing such parameters as learning rate, hidden neurons, momentum, and weights initialization. Two publicly available datasets (the Kaggle Hepatitis Dataset and the UCI Hepatitis Dataset) have been used in this research. Data preprocessing steps including handling missing values, encoding, normalization, and splitting data into train and test datasets were applied. The COA-DNN gave results of 85.11% for accuracy, 77.83% for precision, 83.24% for recall, 79.85% for F1 score, and 0.9054 for AUC on the Kaggle dataset compared to the conventional DNN which had an accuracy of 57.45%. For the UCI dataset, the highest accuracy rate was achieved by COA-DNN at 96.76%, precision of 95.86%, recall of 88.82%, F1 score of 91.94%, and AUC of 0.9793. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Chaotic Optimization Algorithm; Deep Learning; Hepatitis Detection; Hyperparameter Optimization; Multi-Layer Perceptron; Neural.

items.title: Optimizing Agentic Artificial Intelligence to Improve Business Process Automation Efficiency through Modern Digital Technology
items.abstract: In the era of digital transformation, traditional Business Process Automation (BPA) still faces limitations in handling dynamic, unstructured, and complex decision-making tasks. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which is characterized by autonomous agents capable of advanced reasoning, dynamic planning, and multi-step workflow execution, is considered a promising approach to improving the efficiency and adaptability of enterprise operations. This study aims to examine how Agentic AI can be optimized to improve BPA performance within modern digital ecosystems. Using a qualitative approach through a literature study, this paper synthesizes recent academic literature, theoretical models, and technological frameworks related to intelligent automation. The review indicates that integrating Agentic AI into enterprise business architectures has the potential to move beyond rigid, rule-based automation by enabling adaptive problem-solving, real-time context awareness, and cross-system collaboration. The reviewed literature also suggests that autonomous agents may help reduce operational bottlenecks, lower human intervention in routine cognitive workflows, and support more efficient resource allocation across organizational functions. In addition, this study identifies key implementation challenges, including system interoperability, algorithmic transparency, data privacy risks, and the governance mechanisms required for secure deployment. This study contributes to the literature on enterprise automation by proposing strategic considerations for organizations that seek to use digital technology to build more resilient, scalable, and intelligent business processes. Because this is a literature-based study, the findings are conceptual and do not provide empirical evidence of efficiency gains.

items.title: PERSISTENT HOMOLOGY ON LOCAL EXPLANATION SPACES: A TOPOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR EXPLAINABLE AI IN DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: We propose a novel framework that re-architects explainable artificial intelligence within decision support systems by integrating persistent homology into the explanation pipeline. Conventional approaches treat local feature attributions, such as SHAP values, as isolated scalar values for individual predictions, thereby overlooking the multi-scale interaction structures that emerge across a dataset. To address this limitation, we embed a collection of local explanation vectors into a metric space and compute persistent homology using the Vietoris-Rips complex. This topological analysis yields a set of persistence diagrams that capture the birth and death of homology generators across multiple scales. From these diagrams, we construct a global interaction tensor that encodes the total persistence of topological features involving pairs of input features. This tensor is then incorporated into the decision support system’s utility model as a regularization term, which penalizes or rewards the co-occurrence of high-magnitude attributions on features that persistently interact across the dataset. The resulting system provides decision-makers with queryable, multi-scale explanations at selectable persistence thresholds, transforming the interface from a static explainer into a dynamic topological reasoning tool. For instance, a user can request all feature pairs with persistence above a given threshold in a specific homology dimension, and the system highlights those interactions in the explanation. The proposed method is realized using the Ripser algorithm for efficient computation on datasets of up to one hundred thousand instances, with periodic updates via a streaming variant. Our contribution is a principled mathematical framework that bridges topological data analysis and explainable AI, offering a new perspective on feature interaction discovery and explanation stability. The significance lies in its ability to reveal robust, higher-order interaction structures that are invisible to standard attribution methods, thereby enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of model-driven decisions.

items.title: Physics-informed deep learning for few-shot damage localization in carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites under thermal variations
items.abstract: Guided wave (GW)-based damage localization in carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites is fundamentally challenged by thermal variations and sparse sensor configurations, which induce severe baseline distortions and imaging artifacts. Traditional physical algorithms suffer from geometric ambiguity, while purely data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) models are hindered by opaque interpretability and prohibitive data dependency. This paper proposes a physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) framework, an artificial-intelligence-driven approach, for few-shot damage localization under thermal variations. The network is architected with a dual-stream input design, comprising a data-driven layer enhanced by a one-dimensional coordinate attention (1D-CA) mechanism and a physics-informed layer built upon a differentiable time-of-flight (TOF) physical imaging layer. A hybrid physics-constrained loss function is formulated to suppress non-physical artifacts and enforce physical consistency. GW signals are experimentally collected from manufactured CFRP composite plates, and a comparative investigation is performed to thoroughly assess the PIDL performance. Results indicate that:(1) The presence of physical penalties effectively mitigates artifacts and achieves robust localization across thermal gradients; (2) The model demonstrates superior spatial generalization that the integration of acoustic physical constraints acts as a crucial regularization mechanism, maintaining a highly accurate mean relative error (MRE) of 3.88% on completely unseen damage coordinates; (3) By implementing a few-shot transfer learning strategy, the PIDL model shows adaptability for dynamic operational environments (45 degrees Celsius (°C)-75 degrees Celsius (°C)). This work offers a physically interpretable and data-efficient paradigm for structural health monitoring (SHM) in dynamic operational environments.

items.title: Pilot study of a ChatGPT ‐based educational and counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Real-world implementation of large language models such as ChatGPT to enhance patient education remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and attitudes towards a ChatGPT-based counselling tool among patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) in a specialist infectious diseases clinic. METHODS: We conducted a prospective clinical implementation study in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic in Singapore from Jan 2025 to December 2025. Patients interacted with a custom ChatGPT-based chatbot prior to routine counselling by physicians or pharmacists. Responses were reviewed with patients subsequently during consultation. Post-interaction, patients and HCWs completed structured surveys incorporating domains from a validated survey tool: perceived risk, anxiety, technology/social influence and intention for future use. RESULTS: The chatbot was most frequently used for counselling on antiretroviral therapy initiation or switching, and sexual health advice. A total of 35 patients and 35 HCW assessments were analysed. Patients had greater perceived risk with the use of the chatbot compared to HCWs, as indicated by lower median scores (13, IQR 10-16; vs. 18, IQR 15-21), while anxiety scores were similar. Technology/social influence scores were high across both groups (overall median 20, IQR 19-22). Most participants indicated willingness for future use. Qualitative feedback highlighted improved patient understanding and more focused consultations, but concerns included lack of contextual nuance and occasional inaccuracies. CONCLUSIONS: The pilot implementation of a ChatGPT-based counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic was feasible and generally acceptable to patients and HCWs. Further studies are required to evaluate accuracy and clinical effectiveness before broader implementation.

items.title: Prediction of Ischemic Heart Disease with A Hybrid Algorithm of Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Xgboost Using Data from Yazd Health Study (YaHS)
items.abstract: Introduction: Ischemic heart disease represents one of the most prevalent conditions characterized by elevated mortality rates. The aim of this research was to provide an efficient instrument for the early diagnosis of ischemic heart disease and to assist clinical decision-making processes through the application of hybrid artificial intelligence algorithms. Methods: The data used in this study were from Yazd Health Study (YaHS) enrollment phase dataset, comprising 9969 participants and 30 selective features from a total of 300, collected between 2014 to 2015. Data were analyzed using SVM and XGBoost machine learning algorithms using Python version 3.11.8. Results: Combining the strengths of SVM and XGBoost models through a Voting Classifier approach enhanced both the accuracy and efficiency of the heart disease prediction model. When evaluating the predictive performance for heart disease, the Voting Classifier model achieved in accuracy rate of 90%. Conclusion: These findings suggest that implementing machine learning techniques and hybrid algorithms for early diagnosis and prediction could facilitate earlier intervention in CHD, ultimately helping to lower mortality rates.

items.title: Preserving Human Judgment in AI-Enabled Education: The SAM Model for AI Readiness, Assessment, and Human-in-the-Loop Decision Making
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance.

items.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
items.abstract: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

items.title: Psychological correlates of dependence on generative and conversational AI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background. Dependence on generative and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is measured with diverse instruments spanning addiction criteria, task reliance, and emotional bonding. No meta-analysis has pooled its psychological correlates across populations. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered three-level meta-analysis (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23420672) searching eight electronic databases and citations of instrument papers on 16 October 2026, with citation chasing. Zero-order correlations were pooled using correlated and hierarchical effects models on Fisher's z with cluster-robust inference (CR2). Scale type (T1 addiction-type, T2 functional, T3 emotional, T4 mixed) was the primary moderator. Certainty was rated via GRADE. Results. We included 127 samples (123 studies; N = 74,492; 29 countries; 70% university students; 39% mainland China). AI dependence correlated moderately with anxiety (r = 0.37, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48]), stress (r = 0.35 [0.25, 0.43]), depression (r = 0.32 [0.21, 0.42]), social anxiety (r = 0.36 [0.17, 0.53]), loneliness (r = 0.28 [0.18, 0.38]), and procrastination (r = 0.26 [0.12, 0.40]), and weakly and inversely with self-esteem (r = −0.18 [−0.35, −0.00]). All 95% prediction intervals crossed zero. Addiction-type and mixed scales showed no detectable difference; functional and emotional scales were rarely paired with clinical outcomes. Certainty was low to very low. Conclusions. AI dependence moderately correlates with distress and self-regulation difficulties, but prediction intervals cross zero and evidence certainty is low. Functional and emotional dependence have rarely been studied alongside clinical outcomes.

items.title: PUBLIC PERCEPTION AND TRUST IN AI FOR FRAUD DETECTION AND INFLUENCER AUTHENTICITY IN INFLUENCER MARKETING
items.abstract: The rapid growth of influencer marketing has created diverse opportunities for the brands to interact with the consumers. At the same time, concerns regarding manipulated follower counts, artificial engagement and questionable influencer authenticity have become increasingly relevant. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used as a technological mechanism for finding skeptical patterns and supporting fraud detection. However, the use and acceptance of these systems are largely influenced by consumers’ perceptions and trust. The present study focuses trust and concerns of consumers regarding AI-driven fraud detection and consumer attitudes towards transparency, AI-based verification and measures intended to strengthen authenticity in influencer marketing. The study adopts a descriptive research design and uses primary data collected from 70 respondents through a structured questionnaire. The findings show that respondents demonstrate cautious acceptance of AI-driven fraud detection. Half of the respondents reported that they somewhat trust AI, whereas complete trust was comparatively limited. Concerns relating to transparency, privacy, false identification and possible bias were also identified. The findings further reveal that consumers attach considerable importance to transparency and generally support AI-based verification systems. Respondents also expressed favourable opinions regarding the use of AI tools by brands while evaluating influencers for collaboration. The study concludes that AI can contribute to improving authenticity in influencer marketing, but its acceptance depends on the development of transparent, reliable and accountable systems.

items.title: qcGEM: A Graph‐Based Molecular Representation With Quantum Chemistry Awareness
items.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped drug discovery. AI-based models typically rely on molecular representations for prediction. However, the absence of physically grounded information in mainstream molecular representations not only limits the model performance in practical applications but also hinders mechanistic understanding and exploitation by humans. To overcome this issue, we introduce qcGEM, a quantum-chemistry-aware graph-based embedding of molecules that incorporates physical priors into molecular representation learning. Through a specially designed model architecture to adequately process quantum chemistry information, qcGEM provides a compact, physics-informed molecular representation that supports a diverse range of downstream applications. Particularly, qcGEM demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of molecule-related benchmarks, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluations on 83 tasks including molecular property prediction, activity cliff detection, protein-ligand interaction modeling, and opioid drug regression, and simultaneously offers strong interpretability at multiple representation levels. We additionally propose a simplified variant, qcGEM-Hybrid, with substantially accelerated embedding generation and robust performance. Overall, our method provides an advanced molecular representation that will benefit molecule-related modeling and prediction, supporting further progress in AI-aided drug discovery.

items.title: Reforming the Law on Gross Negligence Manslaughter in Healthcare within England and Wales: A Post-Pandemic Evaluation of the Williams and Hamilton Paradigm
items.abstract: There is a deep structural crisis at the intersection of clinical medicine and criminal law in England and Wales. This paper attacks the use of the common law principle of gross negligence manslaughter (GNM) in response to involuntary clinical error and argues that the existing legal framework is driven by an unprincipled regimen of single agency fault. This approach compresses complicated, multi-factorial institutional failures into the sole criminal liability of the practitioner on duty, equating an unfortunate consequence with the blameworthy. Using a dual-axis framework that integrates doctrinal legal analysis with socio-technical systems theory and human factors engineering, this paper analyzes the institutional processes leading to and shaping key judicial decisions and considers the actual nature of health care. This study concludes that current legal approaches do not advance patient safety, and, post- pandemic, contribute to an unacknowledged, destructive diffuse risk for health professionals, ultimately inducing systematic defensive medicine, which in turn creates new safety hazards and fundamentally undermines patient- practitioner interaction. While the principle of a "just culture" has been called for in the context of administrative review, this aspirational goal is systemically undermining by the retributive rules of the criminal justice system. This paper concludes with concrete legal reform suggestions; to both codify a statutory framework and to adopt a subjective recklessness standard, ensuring criminal law responds only to criminal intent and to systemic institutional factors that the system's penal framework fails to address.

items.title: Registered Nurses' Experiences of Clinical Decision‐Making: A Qualitative Descriptive Study to Inform Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Decision Support in Nursing
items.abstract: AIM: To describe registered nurses' experiences of clinical decision-making and identify needs that may inform future development of artificial-intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. DESIGN: A qualitative descriptive study. METHODS: Data were collected between 2022 and 2025 through 16 semi-structured interviews with registered nurses working in inpatient wards at a Finnish university hospital. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Perceived challenges in clinical decision-making were related to organisational issues, multiprofessional collaboration, nurse-patient interactions, professional factors and availability and trustworthiness of data. The findings also identified support needs related to health information management, clinical workflows and quality of nursing care that may inform future artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support system development. CONCLUSION: Nurses experienced multifaceted challenges and needs in clinical decision-making, shaped by organisational, professional, relational and information-related factors. Adoption of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support systems may represent one potential approach to optimising clinical decision-making, improving patient care quality and enhancing workflow efficiency. Realising these opportunities requires coordinated efforts at individual, organisational and societal levels, including competence development, workflow redesign, strong data governance and a culture that fosters trust in technology. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: The findings may inform the future development of artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist was used when reporting the results. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Registered nurses participated in the study. IMPACT: What problem did the study address? This paper addresses existing gaps and unmet needs in nursing clinical decision-making What were the main findings? The main findings highlight several key opportunities for artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research may inform efforts to optimise health information management, streamline clinical workflows and improve the quality of nursing care.

items.abstract: Psychological resilience in elite sport concerns adaptation to sustained and acute demands, not the simple absence of distress. This critical integrative review examines how religious meaning-making and religious coping might interact with mental toughness, challenge appraisal, social resources, and human performance under high-performance conditions. It distinguishes resilience as a dynamic process from mental toughness as a contested psychological construct and separates athlete well-being from competitive outcomes. Evidence is synthesized from sport-specific resilience research, religion-and-sport scholarship, established religious-coping measures, and elite-athlete mental-health literature. A conditional, multidimensional framework is proposed in which personally endorsed beliefs may influence the interpretation of stressors, access to support, and persistence, while spiritual struggle, external religious pressure, or rigid ritual dependence may undermine adaptation. The available literature supports examining these pathways but does not establish that religious affiliation directly improves performance or confers immunity from psychological difficulties. The article develops falsifiable propositions and a research design involving longitudinal measurements, contextual stress exposure, validated comparator measures, objective performance indices, and athlete-led qualitative accounts. Its practical recommendations prioritize autonomy, culturally responsive support, clinical referral where indicated, and avoidance of coercive spiritual practices. No new participants or original experimental data are reported. The proposed framework is a hypothesis for empirical testing rather than a validated screening tool or causal finding. elite athletes; psychological resilience; mental toughness; religious coping; stress appraisal; human performance

items.title: ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN INVESTMENT DECISIONS
items.abstract: Investment behaviour has changed as a result of artificial intelligence (AI), which replaces human judgment with data-driven insights. Investors may analyse big information, spot trends, and optimize portfolios with the help of technologies like machine learning, robo-advisors, and predictive analytics, increasing productivity and lowering emotional biases. Adoption of AI is not without its difficulties, though, such as algorithmic bias, a lack of transparency, expensive costs, and problems with data quality. Automation bias and market volatility may increase if automated systems are overused. This study highlights AI’s impact on investor behaviour and emphasizes the importance of a balanced, responsible approach to effectively integrate AI into investment decision-making processes.

items.abstract: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Banking Services: Benefits, Customer Experience and Challenges This research investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern banking services, with particular emphasis on operational efficiency, customer experience, and emerging challenges. It examines the application of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, intelligent chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated fraud detection, in streamlining banking operations, enhancing service personalisation, improving risk management, and supporting data-driven decision-making. Furthermore, the study evaluates key concerns associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. By assessing both the benefits and limitations of AI integration, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of its implications for the banking sector and highlight the importance of responsible, secure, and customer-centric AI implementation in the evolving financial services landscape.

items.title: Savoir / Action — English Translation (V1)
items.abstract: An AI agent can be given an objective by a human, then search, interpret, plan, use tools, and act before returning a result. The human remains present. But how much of this activity can they still understand, verify, or influence? Savoir / Action begins with this difficulty. The manuscript examines the relationship between the knowledge an AI agent treats as valid, the means it uses to act, and the constraints that shape its trajectory. It asks what human supervision can still mean when control cannot be reduced to permissions, a stop button, or approval of the final result. This reflection grew out of exploratory work conducted within a human–AI dyad. We have chosen to make this origin explicit because it is part of the very question we are examining. We do not claim to have established a theory. We present our thinking as it stands: some distinctions have become clearer, some questions remain open, and several propositions still need to be challenged by other perspectives. This is the canonical English translation of the original French manuscript, first published on 5 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23164286

items.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
items.abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

items.title: Self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms among airport employees across multiple occupational groups: a European cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Objectives. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a significant challenge for companies around the globe, including airport environments. Airport studies are limited and have mostly focused on specific occupational groups, particularly baggage handlers, without considering the whole airport community. The aim of this study was to investigate self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms among airport employees across multiple occupational groups. Methods. This cross-sectional study utilized an adapted version of the Nordic musculoskeletal questionnaire (NMQ) with a pain intensity scale. The study was open to every airport employee from 35 companies who agreed to participate; 847 participants fulfilled the inclusion criteria. In addition, a focus group with seven health and safety (H&S) practitioners and three one-to-one email interviews were conducted. The qualitative data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis (RTA). Results. The most common 12-month prevalence rates were for the neck (49.7%), lower back (47.7%) and shoulder pain (45.7%). Additionally, the results showed that females reported higher symptom prevalence and pain intensity than males. Conclusions. Airport employees’ well-being may be improved through tailored ergonomic interventions, occupation-specific risk assessments, employee education and occupational health support.

items.abstract: SIEGE-1 / SIEGE-1R / SIEGE-2 — the Long Siege battery: six years of simulated attacker evolution thrown at the PORTCULLIS deterministic gate, escalating quantum-capability assumptions each wave (HNDL 2026, NISQ 2027, early fault-tolerance 2028, CRQC-early 2029, full CRQC 2030, CRQC-at-scale 2031), 79+ deterministic adjudications, no LLM in the decision path, preregistration-before-execution. Headline finding: across all six simulated years, no attack derived advantage from quantum capability itself. The gate's PQC material (kyber_1024, CRYSTALS-Dilithium3, SPHINCS+-256f) has no classical residue to break. Every CRQC-era success exploited PRE-QUANTUM trust seams: (C1) the gate trusted a claimed submitter string with no envelope binding; (C2) the pending-ACK queue was shared across submitters, allowing cross-tenant denial of the owner; (C3) the algorithm-role wall was one-directional (signature-class algorithms accepted for KEM-class operations); (C4) per-submitter budgets were trivially evaded by identity rotation. Hardening arc: SIP-030 approved, PORTCULLIS v1.4 built (amendments 10-13: envelope-bound submitter proof, owner-reserved ACK queue with per-submitter caps, bidirectional role wall, aggregate window cap). SIEGE-2 verification: PASS — C1 CLOSED, C2 CLOSED, C3 CLOSED, C4 BOUNDED; regression stayed closed; 4/4 owner controls admitted. Honest disclosures (append-only doctrine): SIEGE-1 run 1 suffered a harness defect (attacker budget exhaustion masked mid-wave seams) — kept unaltered, re-run corrected with fresh identities. SIEGE-2 run 1 flagged FAIL from harness predicate bugs while the gate's verdict column was correct throughout. SIEGE-2 also caught a REAL defect in v1.4 itself before deploy: the original aggregate cap (500) was unreachable in a 250-record window — dead code — reparameterized to 125 and disclosed. Frozen shas: gate v1.3 3726f6a5..., v1.4 2940b768..., allowlist 2c8ff6eb..., keysets 502ef8b0..., prereg 58ab8326... Full SHA256 manifest in the bundle. Deterministic adjudication throughout; forward-only amendments; frozen corpora untouched. items.title: Single-cell morpho-molecular foundation modeling from histopathology with PAST
items.abstract: We present PAST, a single-cell morpho-molecular foundation model trained on ~20 million paired single-cell image–transcriptome instances derived from 49 tissue sections, comprising 42 human sections from 40 independent patients and 7 mouse sections across 15 tumor and tissue contexts. By jointly encoding cellular morphology and gene expression, PAST learns unified cross-modal representations that capture both spatial and molecular heterogeneity at the cellular level, enabling accurate prediction of single-cell gene expression, virtual molecular staining, and multimodal survival analysis directly from routine pathology slides.

items.title: Sustainable and Green Networking: Architectures, Techniques, and Future Directions for Energy-Efficient Communication Infrastructures
items.abstract: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure is rapidly becoming an electrical energy consumer, and an increasingly non-trivial emitter of greenhouse-gases as a result of the growth of global data traffic, cloud computing, artificial-intelligence workloads and always-connected Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices. Sustainable and Green Networking tackles this challenge by building energy-awareness into the design, deployment and operation of communication networks without affecting performance, reliability and quality of service. This paper summarizes the key concepts of green networking derived from literature published from 2022 to 2025, outlines the major classes of energy-saving techniques (standby and sleep modes, rate adaptation, energy-proportional computing, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV) based orchestration, and renewable-powered infrastructure) and suggests a cross-layer conceptual framework that brings these techniques together under a single carbon-intensity feedback loop. As examples of application areas, green 5G/6G radio access networks, sustainable data centers, and energy efficient IoT/edge computing are presented. A comparative study of the energy savings potential reported in the recent literature is presented, followed by a discussion of open challenges in the research field: the performance-energy trade-off, the standardization of energy information exposure, and the AI/ML energy-overhead trade-off, as well as interesting future research directions: the standardization of energy information exposure and the AI-native energy orchestration. The results will inform researchers, network operators and policymakers in their quest for more sustainable digital infrastructures.

items.title: Sustainable Creative Talent Development through Work-Integrated Learning and Industry Engagement
items.abstract: Malaysia’s applied creative arts and media sector is being reshaped by digitalisation, project-based work, and changing industry expectations. However, higher education programmes do not always prepare graduates with the combination of creative, technical, digital, interpersonal, and professional competencies required by the industry. Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) can help address this gap by connecting academic learning with authentic workplace experiences. Nevertheless, WIL in creative arts education is often implemented as a short-term placement rather than as an integrated part of the curriculum. This conceptual paper proposes a stakeholder-informed WIL framework for sustainable creative talent development in Malaysia’s applied creative arts ecosystem. The framework is grounded in Experiential Learning Theory and organised using an Input–Process–Output structure. The inputs consist of industry-required competencies and active industry engagement. The process comprises structured WIL activities, including real-world projects, workplace exposure, industry mentorship, practitioner feedback, reflective learning, and curriculum collaboration. The intended outcomes are stronger employability skills, industry readiness, career adaptability, and sustainable creative talent development. The paper argues that effective WIL requires continuous collaboration among higher education institutions, students, industry practitioners, and policymakers. Its main conceptual contribution is the integration of competency requirements, industry participation, experiential learning, and graduate outcomes within a single framework designed for Malaysia’s applied creative arts sector. The framework offers practical guidance for improving curriculum relevance, clarifying stakeholder responsibilities, strengthening university–industry collaboration, and designing meaningful workplace learning experiences. Ultimately, it provides a foundation for developing adaptable, digitally capable, and future-ready creative graduates who can contribute to Malaysia’s evolving creative economy.

items.abstract: People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. items.title: Syntropic Horizons of Hope — Conscience, Obligation, and Answerable Action
items.abstract: Human responsibility cannot be reduced either to compliance with established obligations or to fidelity to personal conviction. Both individuals and institutions can recognize genuine demands of responsibility, and both can misunderstand the realities to which they respond. This essay develops a philosophy of syntropic praxis in which conscience is understood as a situated, fallible, and cultivable capacity for recognition and judgment. Its exercise depends on disciplined attention, public inquiry, legitimate authority, the claims of others, and responsiveness to consequences. Through encounters with fallibilism, social epistemology, practical wisdom, conscientious objection, civil resistance, epistemic injustice, and artificial intelligence, the essay argues that corrigibility must be cultivated personally and organized institutionally. Syntropic praxis names neither a privileged form of conduct nor a guarantee of moral truth, but an orientation toward more coherent, justifiable, and responsible participation in shared reality.

items.title: Systematic Review of AI-Based PHM Frameworks for Ship Systems and Equipment
items.abstract: Maritime operations require high levels of availability and safety under changing cargo, operational, and environmental conditions. Therefore, anticipating degradation and failures in critical ship systems is an important operational requirement.Although predictive maintenance has advanced rapidly through data-driven approaches and artificial intelligence (AI), the available literature remains fragmented and does not consistently establish the relationships among the ship systems analyzed, the methodological approaches employed, and the conditions required for operational implementation.This article presents a systematic literature review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to examine the development of AI-based predictive maintenance for ship systems from a Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) perspective. Scopus and Web of Science were searched, and predefined screening, eligibility, inclusion, and exclusion criteria were applied.The findings show that research is strongly concentrated on propulsion systems, classified under Ship Work Breakdown Structure (SWBS) Group 200, and electric-plant systems, classified under SWBS Group 300, with most studies focusing on detection and diagnosis. Prognostic and prescriptive applications remain comparatively less developed. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by machine-learning and deep-learning approaches using operational and condition-monitoring variables associated with different operating regimes.Overall, maritime PHM exhibits uneven levels of functional and implementation maturity. Important challenges remain in model comparability, independent validation, and sustained onboard deployment, while opportunities persist for extending PHM to underrepresented ship systems and validating these approaches in real-world fleet operations

items.title: Teaching critical thinking with artificial intelligence: An information literacy training model at the Library of the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing, Universitas Gadjah Mada
items.abstract: Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

items.title: The AI gaze and imagined places: Co-creation and negotiation with the generative AI assemblage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

items.title: The Bargaining-Verification Trap in AI-Mediated Work: An Integrated Theory of Productivity, Worker Voice, and Organisational Resilience
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.

items.title: The Changing Architecture of Intellectual Property in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

items.title: The Effect of Digital Leadership and Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Behavior: An Analysis of Ceo Discourses
items.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

items.title: The Effects of SAP Implementation on Administrative Staff at a Selected South African University of Technology: Developing the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF)
items.abstract: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions such as SAP represent a vital investment for organisations seeking to unify varied operational activities into integrated, data-driven platforms. In institutions of higher learning, the use of ERP systems is a crucial component of digital transformation efforts aimed at improving administrative efficiency, institutional governance, and competitive positioning. This article examines the impact of SAP ERP implementation on both organisational and employee dynamics for administrative staff at the Durban University of Technology (DUT), emphasising technostress, digital fatigue, employee well-being, and post-implementation adaptation within a constrained higher education environment. Utilising a desktop appraisal methodology, the study synthesises existing literature to demonstrate how decisions made in the pre-implementation and implementation phases consistently affect employee experiences and organisational outcomes post-implementation. The study indicates that attaining enduring ERP effectiveness requires continuous capacity development, cooperative implementation approaches, and employee-centered support frameworks. The research develops an interdisciplinary model by integrating socio-technical, psychological, capacity-building, and normalisation perspectives, thereby improving the understanding of the human factors involved in ERP deployment within higher education. The study introduces the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF), which outlines the progressive escalation of technostress during the pre-implementation, implementation, and post-implementation phases, linking each stage to a pertinent theoretical mechanism and a set of organisational interventions. The findings indicate that inadequate training, limited organisational support, dependence on key users, and absence of employee engagement contribute to technostress, digital fatigue, reduced job satisfaction, and challenges in post-implementation adaptation. The study further demonstrates that decisions taken throughout the ERP lifecycle have enduring impacts on employee well-being and organisational effectiveness beyond the system's implementation. This highlights the tangible consequences for higher education institutions, stressing the importance of continuous training, institutional support, systematic information sharing, employee wellness initiatives, and staff-centric ERP management to enhance long-term value achievement. It consequently lays the groundwork for future research on the human dimensions of digital transformation in resource-constrained environments.
